newsitem.title: UK: Major ready for televised British election debates.
newsitem.headline: Major ready for televised British election debates.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, trailing badly in the polls ahead of a British election, has accepted a challenge from Labour leader Tony Blair to televised campaign debates, Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney said on Sunday.

"It's right that there should be a series of debates, at least two," he told BBC television. "We would want them to be prime ministerial debates, and we would want them to include rigorous cross-examination."

The decision by Major, who British newspapers said could announce May 1 as the election date as early as Monday, was seen as a desperate bid to boost the standing of his Conservatives, who are 25 points behind Labour in the latest poll.
But it was immediately challenged by smaller parties.
The third-placed Liberal Democrats said a confrontation from which their leader Paddy Ashdown was excluded would breach rules on political balance which broadcasters must follow during the campaign.
They and the Welsh and Scottish Nationalists said they would mount a legal challenge unless their points of view got an airing.

"We have already been taking legal advice on this," Liberal MP Charles Kennedy said. "The BBC and the other broadcasters would find themselves in a legal minefield if they tried to have a debate...which did not give a voice to the other parties."
Mawhinney said Major had risen to Blair's challenge because he believed Britons should be able to compare the policies of the two most powerful politicians in Britain.

"It is right that the people who have to make that choice should have the opportunity to look at and listen to the two leaders of the parties one of whom would be Prime Minister after the election," Mawhinney said.
Blair, whose party has been out of power since 1979, has never held ministerial office.
Conservative sources said Major's advisers believed he could exploit this inexperience, plus Blair's reluctance to flesh out policy in key areas, during the proposed lengthy debates.

Labour parliamentary business manager Donald Dewar responded enthusiastically. "Dr Mawhinney may be absolutely certain that Mr Blair will be there," he said, although he acknowledged the need to discuss the demands of other parties to participate.
The Liberal Democrats have just 26 seats in the lower House of Commons, and the Scottish and Welsh nationalist four each.
An opinion poll in the Sunday Times newspaper gave Labour 52 percent of the vote against 27 percent for the Conservatives and 13 percent for the Liberals.
Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing in voting patterns among Britain's 44 million electors compared with the last election in 1992 to win an overall majority in parliament.

Historically this would be a huge achievement, but the polls indicate Blair, who has moved his party to the centre ground of politics and ruthlessly exposed Conservative divisions, could pass his target with ease.
Spokesmen for the Conservatives said they could neither confirm nor deny the reports that Major will go to see Queen Elizabeth on Monday to ask for her consent to a May 1 poll.

Televised head-to-head debates between leading candidates are common in U.S. presidential elections but have not been tried previously in Britain where parties run their campaigns mainly through public rallies and party political broadcasts.
